# Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models

Yi Wang Affiliation: ShanghaiTech University    Rui Qian
Affiliation: Fudan University    Yu Li Affiliation: Southeast University
   Haoyang Yao Affiliation: Peking University    Wenjie Wang
Affiliation: ShanghaiTech University

###### Abstract

Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) offer a parameter efficient approach to
scaling reasoning by reusing shared parameters across recurrent
computation steps. Despite their promise, effective post-training of
LoopLMs remains challenging. Existing approaches either provide reward
based supervision that is sparse or costly to extend across loops, or
rely on external teachers or privileged information, leading to limited
teacher availability or teacher-student context mismatch. To address
these limitations, we introduce LoopOPD, a cross-loop on-policy
distillation framework that uses additional recurrent computation within
a LoopLM as its own source of supervision. LoopOPD uses a frozen
terminal loop policy as a compute privileged teacher for an intermediate
loop student on student generated rollouts, providing dense supervision
without an external teacher or privileged information. We further
propose Dynamic LoopOPD (D-LoopOPD), which continually refreshes the
terminal loop teacher as the shared model parameters are updated,
enabling recurrent self-improvement. We characterize how distillation
updates propagate across loop depths and derive sufficient conditions
under which a single update yields simultaneous local improvement at
both loop depths. Experiments on Ouro-Thinking models show that LoopOPD
improves mathematical reasoning, while D-LoopOPD yields further gains
through dynamic teacher updates. Despite being trained only on
mathematical data, the resulting models also improve on general
reasoning and code generation benchmarks, demonstrating that recurrent
computation can serve as an effective source of supervision for LoopLMs.
Our code and model checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.

|     |
| --- |
|     |

## 1 Introduction

Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) have recently received growing
attention as a promising approach to scaling reasoning through recurrent
depth ([Geiping et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)). They reuse shared Transformer
blocks across multiple latent computation steps before emitting each
token ([Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)). This design increases
computational depth without increasing parameter count, leading to
stronger reasoning performance ([Saunshi et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)).
However, effective post-training of LoopLMs remains challenging.
Existing work applies or extends conventional post-training methods to
LoopLMs, including reward based optimization and distillation, but faces
limitations ([Williams et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)).

Specifically, prior work on Ouro, a family of pretrained LoopLMs ([Zhu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)), reports limited gains from reinforcement
learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib11))
over the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) checkpoint. Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO) ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)) assigns reward
credit only to the terminal loop, leaving intermediate latent
computation without direct reward supervision. Reward Latent Thought
Trajectories (RLTT) ([Williams et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)) alleviates
this limitation by extending reward credit across all loops, but
requires retaining per loop log-probabilities, causing memory usage to
scale linearly with the number of loops and thereby limiting long
rollout training. On-Policy Distillation (OPD) ([Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib15)) provides dense distributional supervision but relies
on an external, stronger teacher. For Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, no stronger
same family LoopLM teacher is available, limiting OPD. On-Policy
Self-Distillation (OPSD) instead constructs a same model teacher using
privileged information ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)), but introduces
teacher–student context mismatch ([Kaur et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)).
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
(left) summarizes the three main limitations motivating our work: sparse
terminal loop credit, increasing memory cost across loops, and limited
availability of stronger teachers.

Effective post-training of LoopLMs therefore calls for dense supervision
that directly reaches intermediate loops when no stronger external
teacher is available. Because deeper loops receive more recurrent
computation, the terminal loop naturally provides a stronger policy
within the same model. This raises a question: Can a LoopLM leverage its
own additional recurrent computation to provide such supervision to its
intermediate loops?

To answer this question, we introduce LoopOPD. As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
(right), LoopOPD uses an intermediate loop policy as the student and a
frozen terminal loop policy as the compute privileged teacher. For
student generated rollouts, both policies produce next token
distributions on the same prefixes, and the terminal loop distribution
is distilled into the intermediate loop through OPD. Unlike OPD and
OPSD, the teacher’s advantage arises not from additional parameters ([Li
et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) or privileged information ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12)), but from additional recurrent computation. LoopOPD
therefore turns the model’s own recurrent computation into dense
cross-loop supervision.

Intuitively, because different loops share the same parameters, training
the student also updates the student model’s terminal loop policy,
creating a natural feedback path from the updated terminal policy back
to the student. To exploit this feedback and further strengthen
cross-loop supervision, we propose Dynamic LoopOPD (D-LoopOPD), which
refreshes the terminal loop teacher at each optimization step, as shown
in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
(right). The updated terminal policy then supervises the next student
update, forming a closed teacher-student feedback loop for recurrent
self-improvement. We further analyze cross-loop update transport and
derive sufficient conditions for a single update to induce simultaneous
local descent of task surrogates at both the intermediate and terminal
loops.
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
compares the supervision signals and teacher requirements of these
methods.

We evaluate LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD on Ouro-Thinking ([Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)) across mathematical reasoning ([Zhang and Math-AI,
2026](#bib.bib22)), general reasoning ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib24)), and code generation benchmarks ([Liu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib26)). On mathematical reasoning, both methods outperform
existing baselines on average, with D-LoopOPD further improving over
LoopOPD. Despite training only on mathematical data, they also improve
general reasoning and code generation over the vanilla models.

Figure 1: Existing LoopLM post-training approaches vs. LoopOPD and
D-LoopOPD. Existing approaches variously face sparse supervision,
increasing memory cost across loops, or dependence on stronger external
teachers. LoopOPD uses additional recurrent computation as dense
cross-loop supervision, while D-LoopOPD dynamically refreshes the
terminal loop teacher during training.

Our contributions are threefold:

- •
  We introduce LoopOPD, which uses a frozen terminal loop policy as a
  compute privileged teacher for an intermediate loop student, providing
  dense on-policy supervision without an external teacher or privileged
  information.
- •
  We propose D-LoopOPD, which refreshes the terminal loop teacher at
  each optimization step through shared parameter updates, forming
  recurrent self-improvement. We further analyze cross-loop update
  transport and derive sufficient conditions for local improvement of
  task surrogates at both the intermediate and terminal loops.
- •
  Experiments on Ouro-Thinking models show improved mathematical
  reasoning at both model scales. On Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, D-LoopOPD
  raises terminal loop AIME 2024 Avg@16 from 62.08 to 71.67, with
  cross-loop evaluation showing improvements across all loop depths. The
  resulting models also improve general reasoning and code generation
  despite training only on mathematical data.

## 2 Related Work

Looped and Recurrent-Depth Language Models. Recurrent Transformer
architectures such as the Universal Transformer ([Dehghani et al.,
2019](#bib.bib4)) explore parameter sharing across computational depth.
Recent work studies this principle in language models, showing that
repeated latent computation can improve reasoning and provide an
additional axis for scaling test-time compute ([Saunshi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5); [Geiping et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)). Ouro ([Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)) extends this line of work to pretrained LoopLMs, which
recurrently apply shared Transformer blocks before token generation. Our
work builds on this structure by using additional loop computation as a
source of supervision.

Intermediate Supervision for Recurrent Computation. Recent work develops
training objectives for recurrent latent computation. LSRL ([Ren,
2025](#bib.bib7)) decodes intermediate recurrent states and scores them
with an external grader to provide process supervision. RLTT ([Williams
et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)) extends outcome reward credit from the
terminal loop to intermediate loop distributions in LoopLMs.
LoopRPT ([Tang et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)) uses an EMA teacher and noisy
latent rollouts to construct stepwise reinforcement signals during
pre-training, shaping intermediate representations. These methods
highlight the value of directly supervising intermediate recurrent
computation. Our work provides dense token level supervision to an
intermediate loop using the model’s own terminal loop distribution.

On-Policy Distillation and Self-Distillation. OPD trains a student on
its own trajectories using dense teacher distributions, reducing the
distribution mismatch from off-policy distillation ([Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib15)). Recent analyses identify teacher-student
compatibility and a teacher capability advantage as key factors for
effective OPD ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)). OPSD constructs a teacher
from the same model using privileged information ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12); [Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)), but introduce a
context mismatch that can distort supervision ([Kaur et al.,
2026](#bib.bib17)). In contrast, LoopOPD retains the on-policy setting
and teacher-student compatibility while deriving teacher advantage from
additional recurrent computation, with teacher and student conditioned
on the same context. D-LoopOPD further exploits shared parameters by
refreshing the terminal loop teacher as the model is updated.

| Method                                     | Supervision Signal | No Verifiable Reward | No External Teacher | No Privileged Information | Evolving Teacher |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | -------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------- |
| GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib10))     | Sparse             | $`\times`$           | $`\checkmark`$      | $`\checkmark`$            | –                |
| RLTT ([Williams et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)) | Relatively Dense   | $`\times`$           | $`\checkmark`$      | $`\checkmark`$            | –                |
| OPD ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib15))   | Dense              | $`\checkmark`$       | $`\times`$          | $`\checkmark`$            | $`\times`$       |
| OPSD ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib12))     | Dense              | $`\checkmark`$       | $`\checkmark`$      | $`\times`$                | $`\times`$       |
| LoopOPD                                    | Dense              | $`\checkmark`$       | $`\checkmark`$      | $`\checkmark`$            | $`\times`$       |
| D-LoopOPD                                  | Dense              | $`\checkmark`$       | $`\checkmark`$      | $`\checkmark`$            | $`\checkmark`$   |

Table 1: Comparison of supervision and teacher requirements across
different methods.

## 3 Preliminaries

Looped Language Models. Let $`x`$ be a prompt and
$`y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{m})`$ a generated response of length $`m`$. A
LoopLM recurrently applies shared weight Transformer blocks ([Vaswani et
al., 2017](#bib.bib28); [Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)) for $`L`$
iterations before emitting each token. For the prediction of $`y_{i}`$,
let $`h_{i}^{(d)}`$ denote the hidden state after loop $`d`$. Let
$`\theta`$ denote the parameters of the LoopLM and $`g_{\theta}`$ its
language model head. Applying $`g_{\theta}`$ to the loop $`d`$ hidden
state defines the corresponding next token distribution

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
P_{\theta}^{(d)}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<i})=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(g_{\theta}(h_{i}^{(d)})\right),\qquad d=1,\ldots,L.
``` |  | (1) |

Standard autoregressive generation uses the terminal loop distribution,
inducing the sequence policy

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}P_{\theta}^{(L)}(y_{i}\mid x,y_{<i}).
``` |  | (2) |

For $`d<L`$, we refer to $`P_{\theta}^{(d)}`$ as the intermediate loop
distributions.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). For each prompt $`x`$, GRPO
samples a group of responses $`\{y^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{G}`$ from the old
policy $`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$ and evaluates them with scalar
rewards $`r_{1},\ldots,r_{G}`$. The group relative advantage is
$`\widehat{A}_{j}=(r_{j}-\bar{r})/\sigma_{r}`$. For a LoopLM, response
generation uses the terminal loop distribution, so the token level
importance ratio is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{j,i}(\theta)=\frac{P_{\theta}^{(L)}(y_{i}^{(j)}\mid x,y_{<i}^{(j)})}{P_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}^{(L)}(y_{i}^{(j)}\mid x,y_{<i}^{(j)})}.
``` |  | (3) |

GRPO optimizes the clipped objective

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)={}`$ | $`\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\frac{1}{m_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{j}}\min\!\left(\rho_{j,i}(\theta)\widehat{A}_{j},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{j,i}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\widehat{A}_{j}\right)\right]+\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}),`$ |  | (4) |

where $`\epsilon`$ is the clipping parameter, $`\beta`$ is the KL
coefficient, and $`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ is the reference policy. Thus,
GRPO uses the terminal loop policy for rollouts and direct reward
credit, while gradients propagate through all loops to update the shared
parameters.

Reward Latent Thought Trajectories (RLTT). RLTT extends reward credit
from the terminal loop to all loops while retaining the group relative
advantage ([Williams et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)). Its policy objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RLTT}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\frac{1}{m_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{j}}\sum_{d=1}^{L}\omega_{d}\log P_{\theta}^{(d)}(y_{i}^{(j)}\mid x,y_{<i}^{(j)})\widehat{A}_{j}\right]+\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}),
``` |  | (5) |

where $`\omega_{d}\geq 0`$ and $`\sum_{d=1}^{L}\omega_{d}=1`$. A
limitation of RLTT is that it retain per loop log-probabilities, leading
to memory usage that scales linearly with the number of loops.

On-Policy Distillation (OPD). OPD uses token level teacher distributions
rather than scalar outcome rewards ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib15)).
Let $`\theta`$ and $`\phi`$ denote the parameters of the student LoopLM
and the frozen teacher LoopLM. For $`y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$,
both models are evaluated on the same prefixes $`c_{i}=(x,y_{<i})`$. The
reverse-KL distillation objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta;\phi)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P_{\theta}^{(L)}(\cdot\mid c_{i})\,\middle\|\,P_{\phi}^{(L)}(\cdot\mid c_{i})\right)\right].
``` |  | (6) |

## 4 Method

Prior work reports limited gains from conventional reinforcement
learning post-training on LoopLMs ([Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib9);
[Williams et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)). We explore an intrinsic source of
supervision in LoopLMs: additional recurrent computation. Since a LoopLM
admits a next token distribution at every loop, each loop naturally
induces a corresponding autoregressive policy.

### 4.1 LoopOPD: Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation

For any loop $`d\leq L`$, we define the loop $`d`$ policy as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta}^{(d)}(y\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}P_{\theta}^{(d)}(y_{i}\mid x,y_{<i}).
``` |  | (7) |

As illustrated in
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Dynamic LoopOPD: Recurrent Self-Improvement ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
(left), LoopOPD selects an intermediate loop $`\ell<L`$ as the student
and uses the terminal loop $`L`$ policy as the compute privileged
teacher. We use $`\ell=2`$ and $`L=4`$. Let $`\theta_{0}`$ denote the
initial LoopLM parameters. We initialize the trainable student with
$`\theta\leftarrow\theta_{0}`$ and the frozen teacher with
$`\bar{\theta}_{0}=\theta_{0}`$. For each prompt $`x`$, a response is
sampled from the student policy,

|     |                                          |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       y\sim\pi_{\theta}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\mid x).
       ```                                       |     | (8) |

Both policies are evaluated on the same prefixes $`c_{i}=(x,y_{<i})`$,
and LoopOPD distills the terminal loop distribution into the student
using the reverse-KL objective
in equation [6](#S3.E6 "In 3 Preliminaries ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models"):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LoopOPD}}(\theta;\bar{\theta}_{0})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P_{\theta}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\mid c_{i})\,\middle\|\,P_{\bar{\theta}_{0}}^{(L)}(\cdot\mid c_{i})\right)\right].
``` |  | (9) |

While LoopOPD supervises only the loop $`\ell`$ student policy, the loop
$`\ell`$ and terminal loop policies of the trainable LoopLM share the
same parameters. Updating the student therefore also changes the current
terminal loop policy. Let $`\theta_{t}`$ and $`\theta_{t+1}`$ denote the
parameters before and after optimization step $`t`$. This interaction
can be summarized as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\bar{\theta}_{0}}^{(L)}\xrightarrow{\text{OPD}}\pi_{\theta_{t+1}}^{(\ell)}\xrightarrow{\text{parameter sharing}}\pi_{\theta_{t+1}}^{(L)}.
``` |  | (10) |

### 4.2 Dynamic LoopOPD: Recurrent Self-Improvement

As illustrated in
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Dynamic LoopOPD: Recurrent Self-Improvement ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
(right), D-LoopOPD leverages this shared parameter coupling by using the
current terminal loop policy as the teacher at each optimization step.
Its objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{D\text{-}LoopOPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P_{\theta}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\mid c_{i})\,\middle\|\,\operatorname{sg}\!\left[P_{\theta}^{(L)}(\cdot\mid c_{i})\right]\right)\right],
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\operatorname{sg}[\cdot]`$ denotes stop-gradient. Gradients flow
only through the student distribution, while the shared parameter update
modifies both the loop $`\ell`$ and terminal loop policies. This
interaction can be summarized as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta_{t}}^{(L)}\xrightarrow{\text{OPD}}\pi_{\theta_{t+1}}^{(\ell)}\xrightarrow{\text{parameter sharing}}\pi_{\theta_{t+1}}^{(L)}.
``` |  | (12) |

The updated terminal loop policy then serves as the teacher for the next
optimization step. Repeating this process forms a closed feedback loop
between student learning and teacher evolution, which we refer to as
recurrent self-improvement.

Figure 2: Overview of LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD. LoopOPD uses a frozen
terminal loop policy as a compute-privileged teacher and distills its
next token distribution into an intermediate loop student on student
generated rollouts. D-LoopOPD instead uses the current terminal loop
policy of the same trainable LoopLM as the teacher, so each student
update also changes the teacher used at the next step through shared
parameters, forming recurrent self-improvement.

### 4.3 Theoretical Analysis

We analyze one distillation update and its effect at both loop depths.
At step $`t`$, sample a batch
$`\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{(x^{(j)},y^{(j)})\}_{j=1}^{n_{t}}`$ with
$`y^{(j)}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\mid x^{(j)})`$, response
lengths $`m_{j}\geq 1`$, and prefixes
$`c_{j,i}=(x^{(j)},y_{<i}^{(j)})`$. We hold these sampled tokens and the
targets
$`q_{t}(\cdot\mid c)=\operatorname{sg}[P_{\theta_{t}}^{(L)}(\cdot\mid c)]`$
fixed during the update, as in OPD. The empirical loss retains the
response-wise normalization of
equation [11](#S4.E11 "In 4.2 Dynamic LoopOPD: Recurrent Self-Improvement ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models"):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{t}}\frac{1}{m_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{j}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P_{\theta}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\mid c_{j,i})\,\middle\|\,q_{t}(\cdot\mid c_{j,i})\right),`$ |  | (13) |
|  | $`\displaystyle g_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta_{t}),\qquad\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\eta_{t}g_{t}.`$ |  |  |

where $`g_{t}`$ is the gradient of the empirical distillation loss at
$`\theta_{t}`$, and $`\eta_{t}>0`$ is the step size. We analyze an exact
gradient step for the full-distribution KL objective.

###### Proposition 1 (Descent with a step-frozen teacher).

Suppose $`\mathcal{L}_{t}`$ has an $`M_{t}`$-Lipschitz gradient,
$`M_{t}>0`$, in a neighborhood of the update segment. If $`g_{t}\neq 0`$
and $`0<\eta_{t}<2/M_{t}`$, then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta_{t+1})\leq\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta_{t})-\eta_{t}\!\left(1-\frac{M_{t}\eta_{t}}{2}\right)\!\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2}<\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta_{t}).
``` |  | (14) |

This guarantees a decrease in the batch-averaged KL divergence to the
step-frozen teacher $`q_{t}`$.

For $`d\in\{\ell,L\}`$, concatenate the logits
$`g_{\theta}(h_{i}^{(d)})`$ on the batch prefixes into
$`z_{d}(\theta)`$, and let
$`J_{d}=\partial z_{d}/\partial\theta|_{\theta_{t}}`$ and
$`r_{t}=\nabla_{z_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}_{t}|_{\theta_{t}}`$. With the
teacher stopped, $`g_{t}=J_{\ell}^{\top}r_{t}`$. If the logit maps have
locally Lipschitz Jacobians, then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{d}(\theta_{t+1})-z_{d}(\theta_{t})=-\eta_{t}\underbrace{J_{d}J_{\ell}^{\top}}_{K_{d\ell}}r_{t}+O\!\left(\eta_{t}^{2}\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\right),\qquad d\in\{\ell,L\},
``` |  | (15) |

where $`K_{d\ell}`$ is a block of the empirical tangent kernel ([Jacot
et al., 2018](#bib.bib3)). Parameter sharing gives the first order
terminal logit change $`-\eta_{t}K_{L\ell}r_{t}`$, whose effect on the
task surrogate depends on gradient alignment.

For analysis, let $`\mathcal{R}_{d}(\theta)`$ be a differentiable task
surrogate computed from the logits at loop depth $`d`$ on a fixed
evaluation set $`\mathcal{E}`$, such as gold-token negative
log-likelihood. Define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma_{d,t}=\left\langle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{d}(\theta_{t}),g_{t}\right\rangle,\qquad d\in\{\ell,L\}.
``` |  | (16) |

Here $`\gamma_{d,t}`$ measures the alignment between the distillation
gradient and the task surrogate gradient at depth $`d`$;
$`\gamma_{d,t}>0`$ means that $`-g_{t}`$ is a descent direction for
$`\mathcal{R}_{d}`$.

###### Theorem 1 (Joint local decrease of task surrogates).

Suppose $`\mathcal{R}_{d}`$ has a $`\beta_{d}`$-Lipschitz gradient,
$`\beta_{d}>0`$, in a neighborhood of the update segment for each
$`d\in\{\ell,L\}`$. If $`\gamma_{\ell,t}>0`$, $`\gamma_{L,t}>0`$, and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
0<\eta_{t}<\min_{d\in\{\ell,L\}}\frac{2\gamma_{d,t}}{\beta_{d}\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2}},
``` |  | (17) |

then $`\mathcal{R}_{\ell}(\theta_{t+1})<\mathcal{R}_{\ell}(\theta_{t})`$
and $`\mathcal{R}_{L}(\theta_{t+1})<\mathcal{R}_{L}(\theta_{t})`$
simultaneously.

For evaluation logits $`\widetilde{z}_{d}`$ on $`\mathcal{E}`$, write
$`\widetilde{J}_{d}=\partial\widetilde{z}_{d}/\partial\theta|_{\theta_{t}}`$
and $`a_{d,t}=\nabla_{\widetilde{z}_{d}}\mathcal{R}_{d}|_{\theta_{t}}`$.
Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma_{d,t}=a_{d,t}^{\top}\widetilde{J}_{d}J_{\ell}^{\top}r_{t},\qquad d\in\{\ell,L\}.
``` |  | (18) |

This expression links the training time distillation update to the
evaluation task gradients at both loop depths.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Proofs ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
provides more details.

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

Models. We conduct experiments on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking and
Ouro-2.6B-Thinking ([Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)). For comparison
across model scales, we include Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B ([Yang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib1)), Qwen3.5-4B, and Qwen3.5-9B ([Team,
2026](#bib.bib2)) in thinking mode.

Baselines and Training Dataset. For Ouro, we compare LoopOPD and
D-LoopOPD against GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)),
RLTT ([Williams et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)), and OPSD ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12)). We evaluate OPD ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib15))
on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, using Ouro-2.6B-Thinking as the teacher. For
Qwen3, we evaluate the vanilla models and GRPO variants, while for
Qwen3.5 we evaluate the vanilla models. All post-training methods are
trained on DAPO-Math-17k ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib14)).

Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate mathematical reasoning on AIME
2024 ([Zhang and Math-AI, 2024](#bib.bib20)), AIME 2025 ([Zhang and
Math-AI, 2025](#bib.bib21)), AIME 2026 ([Zhang and Math-AI,
2026](#bib.bib22)), OlympiadBench ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)), and
BeyondAIME ([ByteDance-Seed, 2025](#bib.bib23)). For general reasoning
and code generation, we evaluate on MMLU ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib24)), MBPP and MBPP+ ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib25);
[Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib26)), and HumanEval and HumanEval+ ([Chen et
al., 2021](#bib.bib27); [Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib26)). Detailed
training and evaluation settings are provided in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").

### 5.2 Main Results

Mathematical Reasoning. As shown in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models"),
LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD improve mathematical reasoning on
Ouro-2.6B-Thinking. Averaging Avg@16 across AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and
AIME 2026, the vanilla model and GRPO achieve 55.49 and 56.60, while
LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD improve to 59.37 and 62.36. D-LoopOPD achieves the
best Avg@16 on all three AIME benchmarks within the Ouro-2.6B group,
improving over LoopOPD by 6.46, 1.46, and 1.05 points on AIME 2024, AIME
2025, and AIME 2026, respectively. On AIME 2024, D-LoopOPD reaches 71.67
Avg@16, surpassing vanilla Qwen3-8B at 71.25 and approaching vanilla
Qwen3.5-9B at 72.08 with fewer parameters. On OlympiadBench, D-LoopOPD
also achieves the best result at 65.77, while its BeyondAIME score of
34.00 remains comparable to those of the vanilla model and GRPO. Similar
improvements are observed on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, where LoopOPD and
D-LoopOPD outperform the vanilla model, GRPO, and OPD on average across
the three AIME benchmarks; LoopOPD achieves the best OlympiadBench score
and D-LoopOPD the best BeyondAIME score.

General Reasoning and Code Generation.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
further examines performance beyond mathematical reasoning. On
Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, D-LoopOPD improves over the vanilla model on all
five benchmarks, with gains of 0.58 on MMLU, 1.06 on MBPP, 1.33 on
MBPP+, 0.61 on HumanEval, and 0.61 on HumanEval+. It achieves the best
results within the model group on MMLU, MBPP, and MBPP+. Similar gains
are observed on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, where LoopOPD achieves the best MMLU
result, while D-LoopOPD achieves the best results on MBPP, MBPP+, and
HumanEval+. These gains extend to general reasoning and code generation
even though post-training uses only mathematical data.

### 5.3 Training Dynamics and Cross-Loop Performance

Training Dynamics.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.3 Training Dynamics and Cross-Loop Performance ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
(a) compares LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD during training. Both the rollout
reward and validation performance are measured at the student loop
$`\ell=2`$. D-LoopOPD achieves higher training reward and higher
validation Avg@16 than LoopOPD. These trends support the benefit of
dynamically using the current terminal loop policy as the teacher for
student learning.

![Refer to caption](2610.10623v1/training.png)

Figure 3: Training dynamics and cross-loop performance of
Ouro-2.6B-Thinking. (a) Training reward and student loop validation
Avg@16 for LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD over training. (b) Avg@16 and Pass@16
across loop depths for different methods. All evaluations use a maximum
response length of 31,744 tokens. Exact values are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").

Cross-Loop Performance.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.3 Training Dynamics and Cross-Loop Performance ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
(b) evaluates the trained models across all four loops. Both LoopOPD and
D-LoopOPD improve Avg@16 over the vanilla model at every depth, with
D-LoopOPD achieving the highest Avg@16 among the compared methods. At
the directly supervised loop 2, D-LoopOPD raises Avg@16 from 39.16 to
47.50, a gain of 8.34 percentage points. The gains extend to loops 3 and
4, where Avg@16 increases by 5.41 and 9.59 points to 66.87 and 71.67.
These results support supervising intermediate computation as an
effective way to improve both intermediate and terminal policies.

Teacher and Student Entropy.
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Training Dynamics and Cross-Loop Performance ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
compares the teacher and student token distribution entropy of LoopOPD
and D-LoopOPD during training.

Figure 4: Teacher and student entropy during training for
Ouro-2.6B-Thinking. Left: entropy of the terminal loop teacher. Right:
entropy of the student loop $`\ell=2`$. Both are measured on student
generated rollouts.

D-LoopOPD maintains higher teacher and student entropy than LoopOPD
through most of training, with the gap narrowing toward later steps.
This suggests that dynamically refreshing the terminal loop teacher
maintains less peaked distributions during training, which support more
diverse student rollouts and broader exploration ([Jin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30); [Cui et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)). More details are
provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").

### 5.4 Ablation Study

Figure 5: Student depth ablation for D-LoopOPD on Ouro-2.6B-Thinking.
AIME 2024 Avg@16 at the student and terminal loops.

We study the effect of student depth in D-LoopOPD by using loop 1, loop
2, or loop 3 as the student while keeping the terminal teacher at loop
4. As shown in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.4 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models"),
loop 2 yields the best terminal performance, improving loop 4 Avg@16
from 62.08 to 71.67. Loop 3 already starts close to the initial terminal
policy, with Avg@16 of 61.46 versus 62.08, leaving less room for
distillation. In contrast, loop 1 has a much larger gap to the teacher
but very low standalone accuracy. Its student Avg@16 remains at 0.63
after training, although the terminal loop improves to 68.54. Loop 2
provides a favorable balance between student capability and teacher
advantage: its student Avg@16 improves from 39.16 to 47.50, while the
terminal loop gains 9.59 points. These results indicate that neither a
larger teacher-student gap nor a stronger student alone determines the
effectiveness of cross-loop distillation. Overall, the intermediate loop
$`\ell=2`$ yields the strongest terminal loop improvement in our
setting.

## 6 Conclusion

We propose LoopOPD, which uses a frozen terminal loop policy to
supervise an intermediate loop student through on-policy distillation,
without an external teacher or privileged information. D-LoopOPD instead
uses the current terminal loop policy as the teacher, allowing student
updates to shape subsequent supervision through shared parameters. Our
analysis characterizes this interaction and gives sufficient conditions
for a single gradient update to improve task surrogates locally at both
loop depths. Experiments on Ouro-Thinking models show gains in
mathematical reasoning, with D-LoopOPD further improving mathematical
performance over LoopOPD. Cross-loop evaluation shows that the gains
extend beyond the directly supervised student to deeper loops. D-LoopOPD
also improves general reasoning and code generation over the vanilla
models despite using only mathematical training data. These findings
support additional recurrent computation as an effective source of
supervision for post-training LoopLMs.

## Appendix A Proofs

Scope and Normalization. We condition on the rollout batch
$`\mathcal{B}_{t}`$ in
equation [13](#S4.E13 "In 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
The sampled tokens, response lengths, and teacher probabilities are held
fixed during differentiation. Hidden states and logits on these fixed
token prefixes are functions of the trainable parameters. We use the
reverse KL over the softmax distributions in
equation [1](#S3.E1 "In 3 Preliminaries ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models"),
assuming finite logits and a finite vocabulary so that all probabilities
are positive. Each token occurrence $`(j,i)`$ has weight
$`w_{j,i}=1/(n_{t}m_{j})`$, so that $`\sum_{j}\sum_{i}w_{j,i}=1`$. These
weights match the per response normalization in
equation [11](#S4.E11 "In 4.2 Dynamic LoopOPD: Recurrent Self-Improvement ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").

Reverse-KL Gradient. For a token occurrence $`(j,i)`$, abbreviate

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle p_{j,i}(v)`$ | $`\displaystyle=P_{\theta_{t}}^{(\ell)}(v\mid c_{j,i}),`$ | $`\displaystyle q_{j,i}(v)`$ | $`\displaystyle=q_{t}(v\mid c_{j,i}),`$ |  | (19) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\kappa_{j,i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{j,i}(v)\log\frac{p_{j,i}(v)}{q_{j,i}(v)}.`$ |  |  |  |  |

Let $`z_{\ell,j,i,v}`$ be the corresponding student logit. The block of
$`r_{t}=\nabla_{z_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}_{t}|_{\theta_{t}}`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(r_{t})_{j,i,v}=w_{j,i}p_{j,i}(v)\left(\log\frac{p_{j,i}(v)}{q_{j,i}(v)}-\kappa_{j,i}\right).
``` |  | (20) |

To verify this, use
$`\partial p(u)/\partial z_{v}=p(u)(\mathbf{1}\{u=v\}-p(v))`$ and
$`\partial D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)/\partial p(u)=\log(p(u)/q(u))+1`$.
Summing over $`u`$ gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{\partial D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)}{\partial z_{v}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=p(v)\left(\log\frac{p(v)}{q(v)}+1\right)-p(v)\sum_{u}p(u)\left(\log\frac{p(u)}{q(u)}+1\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=p(v)\left(\log\frac{p(v)}{q(v)}-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\right).`$ |  |

Multiplying by $`w_{j,i}`$ proves
equation [20](#A1.E20 "In Appendix A Proofs ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
Since $`q_{t}`$ is stopped, the chain rule gives
$`g_{t}=J_{\ell}^{\top}r_{t}`$.

Proof of
Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Descent with a step-frozen teacher). ‣ 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
For a differentiable function $`F`$ with an $`M`$-Lipschitz gradient in
a neighborhood of the segment from $`\theta`$ to $`\theta+\Delta`$, the
fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle F(\theta+\Delta)-F(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\langle\nabla F(\theta),\Delta\rangle+\int_{0}^{1}\langle\nabla F(\theta+s\Delta)-\nabla F(\theta),\Delta\rangle\,ds`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\langle\nabla F(\theta),\Delta\rangle+\frac{M}{2}\|\Delta\|_{2}^{2}.`$ |  | (21) |

Apply
equation [21](#A1.E21 "In Appendix A Proofs ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
at $`\theta=\theta_{t}`$ with $`F=\mathcal{L}_{t}`$ and
$`\Delta=-\eta_{t}g_{t}`$. Since
$`\nabla\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta_{t})=g_{t}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta_{t+1})`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta_{t})-\eta_{t}\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{M_{t}\eta_{t}^{2}}{2}\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta_{t})-\eta_{t}\left(1-\frac{M_{t}\eta_{t}}{2}\right)\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2}.`$ |  |

Since $`g_{t}\neq 0`$ and $`0<\eta_{t}<2/M_{t}`$,
$`\eta_{t}(1-M_{t}\eta_{t}/2)\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2}>0`$, proving
equation [14](#S4.E14 "In Proposition 1 (Descent with a step-frozen teacher). ‣ 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").

Proof of
equation [15](#S4.E15 "In 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
For $`d\in\{\ell,L\}`$, assume $`z_{d}`$ is differentiable and its
Jacobian is $`C_{d}`$-Lipschitz in operator norm in a neighborhood of
the update segment. Let
$`J_{d}(\theta)=\partial z_{d}(\theta)/\partial\theta`$, with
$`J_{d}=J_{d}(\theta_{t})`$. Integration gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{d}(\theta_{t}+\Delta)-z_{d}(\theta_{t})-J_{d}\Delta=\int_{0}^{1}\bigl(J_{d}(\theta_{t}+s\Delta)-J_{d}\bigr)\Delta\,ds.
``` |  | (22) |

The norm of the right-hand side is at most
$`C_{d}\|\Delta\|_{2}^{2}/2`$. With $`\Delta=-\eta_{t}g_{t}`$ and
$`g_{t}=J_{\ell}^{\top}r_{t}`$, this gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\left\|z_{d}(\theta_{t+1})-z_{d}(\theta_{t})+\eta_{t}J_{d}J_{\ell}^{\top}r_{t}\right\|_{2}\leq\frac{C_{d}\eta_{t}^{2}}{2}\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2},
``` |  | (23) |

and hence
equation [15](#S4.E15 "In 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
The joint empirical tangent kernel has the block form

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{bmatrix}J_{\ell}J_{\ell}^{\top}&J_{\ell}J_{L}^{\top}\\
J_{L}J_{\ell}^{\top}&J_{L}J_{L}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}J_{\ell}\\
J_{L}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}J_{\ell}\\
J_{L}\end{bmatrix}^{\!\top}.
``` |  | (24) |

Thus, $`K_{L\ell}=J_{L}J_{\ell}^{\top}`$ is the cross-loop block of the
empirical tangent kernel ([Jacot et al., 2018](#bib.bib3)).

Proof of
Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 (Joint local decrease of task surrogates). ‣ 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
For each $`d\in\{\ell,L\}`$, apply
equation [21](#A1.E21 "In Appendix A Proofs ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
at $`\theta=\theta_{t}`$ with $`F=\mathcal{R}_{d}`$ and
$`\Delta=-\eta_{t}g_{t}`$. This gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}_{d}(\theta_{t+1})-\mathcal{R}_{d}(\theta_{t})\leq-\eta_{t}\gamma_{d,t}+\frac{\beta_{d}\eta_{t}^{2}}{2}\|g_{t}\|_{2}^{2}.
``` |  | (25) |

Since $`\gamma_{\ell,t}>0`$ and $`\gamma_{L,t}>0`$, the step-size
condition in
equation [17](#S4.E17 "In Theorem 1 (Joint local decrease of task surrogates). ‣ 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
makes the right-hand side strictly negative for both $`d\in\{\ell,L\}`$,
proving
Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 (Joint local decrease of task surrogates). ‣ 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").

Proof of
equation [18](#S4.E18 "In 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
Let $`\widetilde{z}_{d}`$ concatenate the logits on the fixed evaluation
set $`\mathcal{E}`$, and let
$`\widetilde{J}_{d}=\partial\widetilde{z}_{d}/\partial\theta|_{\theta_{t}}`$
and $`a_{d,t}=\nabla_{\widetilde{z}_{d}}\mathcal{R}_{d}|_{\theta_{t}}`$.
By the chain rule,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma_{d,t}=\bigl(\widetilde{J}_{d}^{\top}a_{d,t}\bigr)^{\top}J_{\ell}^{\top}r_{t}=a_{d,t}^{\top}\widetilde{J}_{d}J_{\ell}^{\top}r_{t},\qquad d\in\{\ell,L\},
``` |  | (26) |

which proves
equation [18](#S4.E18 "In 4.3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").

Cross-Loop Gradient Alignment. Consider binary next token prediction
with a shared recurrent map and output head. Let token $`1`$ be correct,
with logits $`(a,0)`$ and probability $`\sigma(a)=(1+e^{-a})^{-1}`$. In
both examples, we use a single fixed prefix $`c`$ with unit weight, only
the scalar parameter $`\theta`$ is trainable, and take

|     |                                                          |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{R}_{d}(\theta)=-\log P_{\theta}^{(d)}(1\mid c).
       ```                                                       |     |

For a positively aligned case, let $`h^{(0)}=0`$,
$`h^{(k)}=h^{(k-1)}+\theta`$, and use logits $`(h^{(d)},0)`$. Take
$`\ell=2`$, $`L=4`$, and $`\theta_{t}>0`$. Then
$`p=\sigma(2\theta_{t})`$ and $`q=\sigma(4\theta_{t})>p`$. The
stopped-target reverse-KL gradient is

|     |                                           |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       g_{t}=2p(1-p)(2\theta_{t}-4\theta_{t})<0.
       ```                                        |     | (27) |

Thus a gradient step increases $`\theta`$, increasing the correct token
probabilities at both depths and decreasing both negative
log-likelihoods. For a contrasting case, consider

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
h^{(0)}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\
0\end{bmatrix},\qquad h^{(k)}=Ah^{(k-1)}+\theta\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix},\qquad A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\
1&-1\end{bmatrix},
``` |  | (28) |

with the shared head $`g(h)=((1,-2)h,0)`$. Direct substitution gives
$`h^{(2)}=(\theta,\theta)^{\top}`$ and $`h^{(4)}=(\theta,0)^{\top}`$, so
the correct token logits are $`-\theta`$ at loop $`2`$ and $`\theta`$ at
loop $`4`$. At $`\theta_{t}=1`$, $`p=\sigma(-1)<q=\sigma(1)`$. The
stopped-target gradient is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{t}=-p(1-p)(-1-1)=2p(1-p)>0,\qquad\theta_{t+1}=1-\eta_{t}g_{t}<1.
``` |  | (29) |

The student probability $`\sigma(-\theta)`$ increases while the terminal
probability $`\sigma(\theta)`$ decreases. Moreover,
$`\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{\ell}(1)=1-p>0`$ and
$`\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{L}(1)=q-1<0`$, giving $`\gamma_{\ell,t}>0`$ and
$`\gamma_{L,t}<0`$. Thus, a stronger terminal teacher does not by itself
imply $`\gamma_{L,t}>0`$.

## Appendix B Algorithms

Algorithms [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix B Algorithms ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
and [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix B Algorithms ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
describe the training procedures in
Sections [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 LoopOPD: Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
and [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Dynamic LoopOPD: Recurrent Self-Improvement ‣ 4 Method ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
Each iteration samples $`G`$ responses for each of $`B`$ prompts, giving
$`n_{t}=BG`$ responses. Teacher and student distributions are computed
on the same student generated prefixes. $`\operatorname{OptimizerStep}`$
denotes one update with the chosen optimizer.

1: Training prompts $`\mathcal{D}`$; initial parameters $`\theta_{0}`$;
student depth $`\ell<L`$; terminal depth $`L`$; prompt batch size $`B`$;
rollouts per prompt $`G`$; number of updates $`T`$; learning rates
$`\{\eta_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}`$; optimizer.

2: Trained parameters $`\theta_{T}`$, defining
$`\pi_{\theta_{T}}^{(\ell)}`$ and $`\pi_{\theta_{T}}^{(L)}`$.

3: Initialize the trainable LoopLM with $`\theta_{0}`$.

4: Create a frozen teacher copy with
$`\bar{\theta}_{0}\leftarrow\theta_{0}`$.

5: for $`t=0,\ldots,T-1`$ do

6:   Student rollouts

7:   Draw $`B`$ prompts $`x_{1},\ldots,x_{B}`$ from $`\mathcal{D}`$.

8:   for $`b=1,\ldots,B`$ do

9:    Sample
$`y^{(b,s)}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\mid x_{b})`$,
$`s=1,\ldots,G`$.

10:   end for

11:   Flatten the responses into
$`\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{(x^{(j)},y^{(j)})\}_{j=1}^{n_{t}}`$, where
$`n_{t}=BG`$.

12:   Set $`m_{j}\leftarrow|y^{(j)}|`$ and
$`c_{j,i}\leftarrow(x^{(j)},y_{<i}^{(j)})`$ for $`j=1,\ldots,n_{t}`$,
$`i=1,\ldots,m_{j}`$.

13:   Frozen teacher targets

14:   Evaluate the frozen teacher at depth $`L`$ on the batch prefixes.

15:   $`q_{j,i}(v)\leftarrow P_{\bar{\theta}_{0}}^{(L)}(v\mid c_{j,i})`$
for all $`(j,i)`$ and $`v\in\mathcal{V}`$.

16:   Evaluate the trainable LoopLM at depth $`\ell`$ on the same
prefixes.

17:   $`p_{j,i}(v)\leftarrow P_{\theta_{t}}^{(\ell)}(v\mid c_{j,i})`$
for all $`(j,i)`$ and $`v\in\mathcal{V}`$.

18:
  $`\displaystyle\kappa_{j,i}\leftarrow\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{j,i}(v)\log\frac{p_{j,i}(v)}{q_{j,i}(v)}`$
for all $`(j,i)`$.

19:
  $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}\leftarrow\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{t}}\frac{1}{m_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{j}}\kappa_{j,i}`$.

20:
  $`g_{t}\leftarrow\left.\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{t}\right|_{\theta=\theta_{t}}`$.

21:
  $`\theta_{t+1}\leftarrow\operatorname{OptimizerStep}(\theta_{t},g_{t},\eta_{t})`$.

22: end for

23: return $`\theta_{T}`$.

Algorithm 1 LoopOPD: Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation

1: Training prompts $`\mathcal{D}`$; initial parameters $`\theta_{0}`$;
student depth $`\ell<L`$; terminal depth $`L`$; prompt batch size $`B`$;
rollouts per prompt $`G`$; number of updates $`T`$; learning rates
$`\{\eta_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}`$; optimizer.

2: Trained parameters $`\theta_{T}`$, defining
$`\pi_{\theta_{T}}^{(\ell)}`$ and $`\pi_{\theta_{T}}^{(L)}`$.

3: Initialize the trainable LoopLM with $`\theta_{0}`$.

4: for $`t=0,\ldots,T-1`$ do

5:   Student rollouts

6:   Draw $`B`$ prompts $`x_{1},\ldots,x_{B}`$ from $`\mathcal{D}`$.

7:   for $`b=1,\ldots,B`$ do

8:    Sample
$`y^{(b,s)}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\mid x_{b})`$,
$`s=1,\ldots,G`$.

9:   end for

10:   Flatten the responses into
$`\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{(x^{(j)},y^{(j)})\}_{j=1}^{n_{t}}`$, where
$`n_{t}=BG`$.

11:   Set $`m_{j}\leftarrow|y^{(j)}|`$ and
$`c_{j,i}\leftarrow(x^{(j)},y_{<i}^{(j)})`$ for $`j=1,\ldots,n_{t}`$,
$`i=1,\ldots,m_{j}`$.

12:   Current teacher targets

13:   Evaluate the trainable LoopLM at depth $`L`$ on the batch
prefixes.

14:
  $`q_{j,i}(v)\leftarrow\operatorname{sg}\!\left[P_{\theta_{t}}^{(L)}(v\mid c_{j,i})\right]`$
for all $`(j,i)`$ and $`v\in\mathcal{V}`$.

15:   Evaluate the trainable LoopLM at depth $`\ell`$ on the same
prefixes.

16:   $`p_{j,i}(v)\leftarrow P_{\theta_{t}}^{(\ell)}(v\mid c_{j,i})`$
for all $`(j,i)`$ and $`v\in\mathcal{V}`$.

17:
  $`\displaystyle\kappa_{j,i}\leftarrow\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{j,i}(v)\log\frac{p_{j,i}(v)}{q_{j,i}(v)}`$
for all $`(j,i)`$.

18:
  $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}\leftarrow\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{t}}\frac{1}{m_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{j}}\kappa_{j,i}`$.

19:
  $`g_{t}\leftarrow\left.\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{t}\right|_{\theta=\theta_{t}}`$.

20:
  $`\theta_{t+1}\leftarrow\operatorname{OptimizerStep}(\theta_{t},g_{t},\eta_{t})`$.

21:   Use $`\pi_{\theta_{t+1}}^{(L)}`$ as the teacher for the next
iteration.

22: end for

23: return $`\theta_{T}`$.

Algorithm 2 D-LoopOPD: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation

Response Length and Truncation Rate.
Figure [6](#A3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ C.1 Additional Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
compares response length during training, while
Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ C.1 Additional Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
reports the rollout truncation rate. Due to the GPU memory overhead of
retaining learning signals across recurrent loops, we follow the
original RLTT training configuration and use a maximum rollout length of
2,048 tokens for RLTT, while LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD use 31,744 tokens.
RLTT produces substantially shorter responses and exhibits a
substantially higher truncation rate throughout training. In contrast,
LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD generate much longer responses while maintaining
near zero truncation. This behavior is consistent with the decode budget
results in
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Effect of Decode Budget ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models"),
where RLTT performs strongly under short decode budgets but saturates as
the budget increases, while D-LoopOPD continues to benefit from longer
generation. Training RLTT with 31,744 token rollouts exceeded our
available memory budget, highlighting the practical limitation of
extending per loop reward supervision to long rollouts.

Figure 6: Response length during training for Ouro-2.6B-Thinking. Left:
LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD. Right: RLTT. LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD use a maximum
rollout length of 31,744 tokens, while RLTT uses 2,048 tokens.

Figure 7: Rollout truncation rate during training for
Ouro-2.6B-Thinking. RLTT exhibits substantially higher truncation than
LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD throughout training.

### C.3 Effect of Decode Budget

Figure [8](#A3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ C.3 Effect of Decode Budget ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
shows AIME 2024 Avg@16 of Ouro-2.6B-Thinking under different maximum
decode budgets, with exact values reported in
Table [6](#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ C.3 Effect of Decode Budget ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
RLTT performs better under short decode budgets, but its gains diminish
as the budget increases. D-LoopOPD overtakes RLTT at 16K tokens and
continues to improve at 31K, reaching 71.67 Avg@16 compared with 56.67
for RLTT. Notably, RLTT also falls below the vanilla model at both 16K
and 31K, indicating a degradation in its ability to benefit from longer
reasoning trajectories. In contrast, D-LoopOPD exceeds the vanilla model
across all decode budgets and outperforms it from 2K onward, suggesting
that its gains do not come at the cost of long budget reasoning
capability. These results are consistent with the response length and
truncation behavior in
Figures [6](#A3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ C.1 Additional Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
and [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ C.1 Additional Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Experiments ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models"):
RLTT favors short generation under its constrained rollout budget,
whereas D-LoopOPD continues to benefit from longer generation.

Figure 8: Effect of decode budget on AIME 2024 performance for

ranging from 1K to 31K tokens.

| RLTT      | 4.38 | 23.33 | 34.16 | 45.21 | 53.95 | 56.67 |

## Appendix D Implementation Details

### D.1 Training Configuration

We detail the training configurations used throughout our experiments in
Table [7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ D.1 Training Configuration ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
All post-training methods use DAPO-Math-17k as the training dataset,
with its basic statistics summarized in
Table [8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ D.1 Training Configuration ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models").
Each training run uses 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. For OPSD, we follow the
original setup, using a maximum sequence length of 20,000 and a maximum
rollout length of 1,024 tokens. RLTT uses a maximum rollout length of
2,048 tokens and AdamW8bit, following its original training
configuration, consistent with the higher GPU memory usage associated
with retaining learning signals across recurrent loops. We use uniform
weights across recurrent loops. LoopOPD and D-LoopOPD use student depth
$`\ell=2`$ and terminal depth $`L=4`$.

### D.2 Evaluation Protocol

Table [9](#A4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ D.2 Evaluation Protocol ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models")
summarizes the evaluation protocols used throughout our experiments. For
mathematical reasoning benchmarks, we use zero-shot generation with
thinking enabled. For MMLU, we use the standard 5-shot multiple-choice
log-likelihood evaluation, while code generation benchmarks are
evaluated using EvalPlus.

Mathematical Reasoning. For all mathematical reasoning benchmarks, each
example is provided as a single user message containing the original
problem followed by:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and AIME 2026, we evaluate all 30 problems
from each benchmark under the same protocol. Each problem is evaluated
with 16 sampled completions using temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p`$
$`0.7`$, and a maximum of 31,744 generated tokens. We extract the final
boxed answer and determine correctness using numerical and symbolic
mathematical equivalence. We report two metrics. Avg@16 is the fraction
of correct completions among the $`30\times 16=480`$ generated responses
for each benchmark. Pass@16 is the fraction of the 30 problems for which
at least one of the 16 completions is correct.

For OlympiadBench, we evaluate 675 text-based mathematical problems. For
BeyondAIME, we use the official test split containing 100 problems. Both
benchmarks use temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p`$ $`0.7`$, and a maximum of
31,744 generated tokens.

MMLU. We evaluate MMLU using lm-eval-harness on the full test split of
14,042 questions across 57 subjects. We use five demonstrations from the
development split of each subject together with the subject description.
The prompt is formatted as:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We select the candidate with the highest log-likelihood among A, B, C,
and D.

Code Generation. We evaluate MBPP, MBPP+, HumanEval, and HumanEval+
using EvalPlus. MBPP and MBPP+ contain 378 problems, while HumanEval and
HumanEval+ contain 164 problems. For each problem, we generate one
program and use it to compute both the original and “+” benchmark
scores. The original benchmark uses the base test suite, while the “+”
variant additionally includes the extended tests. We use greedy decoding
with one generated solution per problem and a maximum of 768 new tokens.
The prompt is formatted as:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Benchmark | \# Examples | Decoding / Scoring | Max New Tokens | Metric |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| AIME 2024 | 30 | $`T=1.0`$, $`p=0.7`$, $`n=16`$ | 31,744 | Avg@16 / Pass@16 |
| AIME 2025 | 30 | $`T=1.0`$, $`p=0.7`$, $`n=16`$ | 31,744 | Avg@16 / Pass@16 |
| AIME 2026 | 30 | $`T=1.0`$, $`p=0.7`$, $`n=16`$ | 31,744 | Avg@16 / Pass@16 |
| OlympiadBench | 675 | $`T=1.0`$, $`p=0.7`$, $`n=1`$ | 31,744 | Accuracy |
| BeyondAIME | 100 | $`T=1.0`$, $`p=0.7`$, $`n=1`$ | 31,744 | Accuracy |
| MMLU | 14,042 | Candidate log-likelihood | – | Accuracy |
| MBPP | 378 | Greedy, $`n=1`$ | 768 | Pass@1 |
| MBPP+ | 378 | Greedy, $`n=1`$ | 768 | Pass@1 |
| HumanEval | 164 | Greedy, $`n=1`$ | 768 | Pass@1 |
| HumanEval+ | 164 | Greedy, $`n=1`$ | 768 | Pass@1 |

Table 9: Evaluation settings for different benchmarks.
````
